prize_parts.citation: For the invention of the optical lattice clock based on magic-wavelength trapping and its development to fractional uncertainties near 10^-18

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single prize for the optical lattice clock to Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. The round-1 exchange strengthened it rather than weakening it. Seven of eight members reached the same configuration from different starting points, but I do not rely on that count. What matters is that nobody raised a doubt about reproducibility or maturity: clocks near 1e-18 are operated and intercompared in several independent laboratories. The idea is specific and traceable. Katori's magic-wavelength trapping removes the trade-off between atom number and motional or light-shift systematics, and Ye's programme took the strontium clock to record accuracy and stability. On the chair's scope question, the lattice clock is distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 prize for control of single quantum systems and ion clocks. The comb is the tool that counts optical cycles and the ion-control prize concerns a single trapped quantum system. The lattice clock is a different principle: a large ensemble of neutral atoms interrogated simultaneously in a state-independent trap, which makes the statistical gain and the systematic control compatible. I would put it to the committee as an invention that has already produced new physics, namely constraints on drift of constants, millimetre-scale gravitational redshift measurements and many-body effects in the clock ensemble. It should not be framed only as a future capability. I would word the citation around the lattice clock itself and not around precision spectroscopy in general, so it does not claim the neighbouring work already honoured.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains category. A committee that insists on a newly discovered phenomenon will see an instrument and metrology achievement, and some of its largest consequences, such as redefining the second, relativistic geodesy and dark-matter or constant-drift searches, are still prospective. Attribution at the margin is real: Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Sterr and Gill contributed to the early strontium demonstrations and the stability record, and a two-name prize cannot reflect them. I also cannot rule out that my judgement of the metrology case is coloured by my own field. Finally, the 1e-18 figures and the chronology of the first lattice clocks are recalled, not checked against primary intercomparisons, and the citation should be fixed only after such a check.

responses.point: Danielsson is the only member preferring B022 (MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Bistritzer) and frames the choice against B025 as discovery versus capability, arguing that an unsettled pairing mechanism should not delay recognition of a secure phenomenon.
responses.response: I take the discovery-versus-capability framing seriously and I agree that B022 is the most surprising new phenomenon on the list. I also agree with you that the pairing mechanism need not be settled for a citation worded around the prediction and the observation, and that Bistritzer must not be dropped, since the 2011 continuum model is a two-author paper. Where I still differ is on what the committee can defend this year. For B022 the phenomenology is secure, but the phase diagram, the sample and twist-angle dependence and the credit beyond Jarillo-Herrero (Cao, Fatemi, and the Dean, Young and Kim groups) are all unsettled, and a three-name prize would have to leave out a large part of the experimental community. For B025 the same questions have clean answers. I therefore keep B022 as my first alternative and would not call it premature, but I rank it behind the clock on maturity and attribution. I would also say that the clock is not only a capability: it has already delivered measurements of physics that were not accessible before.

responses.point: Lindroth wants the citation and deliberation to acknowledge the contributions of Lemonde, the SYRTE group and the ion-clock lineage explicitly, and she was asked whether Ye's role is better described as an accuracy and many-body programme or as a distinct invention.
responses.response: I agree that the committee should record the SYRTE and other early strontium contributions in its deliberation, and that the citation must not overclaim the whole field. I would go a little further on the second question. Ye's role is more than an accuracy programme: the cavity-stabilised ultranarrow clock laser, the control of collisional and spin-exchange shifts in a degenerate Fermi gas and the lattice-clock many-body physics are what made 1e-18 operation possible, so I would treat it as a distinct experimental advance on top of Katori's concept. I still hold that the two-name credit is defensible. The concept (Katori) and the record performance (Ye) are each clearly traceable to one person, and the supporting contributions refine the picture without displacing either of them. I would accept a deliberation note on Lemonde and the other groups but not a change of the credited names. Your point on atomic structure also stays with me: the claim of 1e-18 is meaningful only because polarisabilities and blackbody shifts are understood at that level.

responses.point: Kroll cites the Charpak and Hall-Haensch precedents for rewarding measurement inventions, treats the thorium nuclear clock as not yet mature enough to split Ye's credit, and asks the committee to judge his Boulder and WACQT proximity.
responses.response: I agree with your precedent argument and with your handling of the nuclear clock, and I would add that the nuclear-clock question is a reason for caution only if that work matures within the next cycle or two, which I do not expect. On your correction about my earlier circuit QED list, you are right that I left out Wallraff and that neither three-name cut of B016 is clean. That, together with the 2025 scope question and my own proximity, is why I no longer advocate B016 and will stand back from it. On disclosures, I do not see your Boulder stay as a reason to recuse on B025, since no direct tie to Katori or Ye is documented. I would apply the same standard to myself: my WACQT role and Chalmers connections concern B016, not the lattice clock, and I do not think they require stepping back from B025.

responses.point: Olsson proposes that the 1e-18 uncertainty figures and the chronology of the first lattice clocks be verified against primary intercomparisons before the citation is fixed, and she has disclosed a possible institutional link to Katori's country.
responses.response: I support the verification step. Several of us, myself included, are working from recalled values, and a prize citation that states a figure should state one the committee has checked against the published intercomparisons. I would keep the wording tolerant, 'near 10^-18', until that is done. On your disclosure, a JSPS or University of Tokyo fellowship without a documented collaboration with Katori or Ye does not seem to me to require recusal, but it is for the committee to record it. I also note your own candour that B008 has only your support. I agree that the electron-microscope corrector is a clean invention, but as Lindroth also noted, its scientific payoff is spread across materials science and the lattice clock feeds back directly into fundamental physics.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept the distinction from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes (ensemble of neutral atoms in a state-independent lattice, as opposed to the comb as a counter or a single trapped ion).
How far to acknowledge Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Sterr and Gill in deliberation without changing the two credited names.
Whether the 1e-18 figures and the chronology hold up against primary intercomparisons, which I have not verified.
Whether a later thorium nuclear-clock decision would involve Jun Ye again, which I judge unlikely to matter in this cycle.
Whether B022 would have its pairing-mechanism and credit questions sufficiently settled to overtake the clock in a later year.
statement.conflict_note: My profile records that I am a professor at Chalmers and director of WACQT, with documented collaborations with Per Delsing, C. M. Wilson and Anton Frisk Kockum, and that Chalmers hosted researchers associated with the 2025 prize. I should stand back from any discussion of B016, circuit QED, and I no longer advocate it. My profile records no connection to Katori, Jun Ye or the lattice-clock groups, so no conflict is apparent for B025. I also record that I work in a neighbouring quantum-technology area, which may colour my view of metrology.
